In [[applied mathematics]], '''Wahba's problem''', first posed by [[Grace Wahba]] in 1965, seeks to find a [[rotation matrix]] ([[Orthogonal matrix|special orthogonal matrix]]) between two coordinate systems from a set of (weighted) vector observations. Solutions to Wahba's problem are often used in [[satellite]] [[attitude determination]] utilising sensors such as [[magnetometer]]s and multi-antenna [[Global Positioning System|GPS receivers]]. The cost function that Wahba's problem seeks to minimise is as follows:

: <math>J(\mathbf{R}) = \frac{1}{2} \sum_{k=1}^{N} a_k\| \mathbf{w}_k - \mathbf{R} \mathbf{v}_k \|^2 </math> for <math>N\geq2 </math>

where <math>\mathbf{w}_k</math> is the ''k''-th 3-vector measurement in the reference frame, <math>\mathbf{v}_k</math> is the corresponding ''k''-th 3-vector measurement in the body frame and <math>\mathbf{R}</math> is a 3 by 3 rotation matrix between the coordinate frames.<ref>The rotation <math>\mathbf{R}</math> in the problem's definition transforms the body frame to the reference frame. Most publications define rotation in the reverse direction, i.e. from the reference to the body frame which amounts to <math>\mathbf{R}^T</math>.</ref>
<math>a_k</math> is an optional set of weights for each observation.

A number of solutions to the problem have appeared in literature, notably Davenport's q-method,<ref>{{Cite web |title=Davenport's Q-method (Finding an orientation matching a set of point samples) |url=https://math.stackexchange.com/q/1634113 |access-date=2020-07-23 |website=Mathematics Stack Exchange}}</ref> [[quaternion estimator algorithm|QUEST]] and methods based on the [[singular value decomposition]] (SVD). Several methods for solving Wahba's problem are discussed by Markley and Mortari.

This is an alternative formulation of the [[orthogonal Procrustes problem]] (consider all the vectors multiplied by the square-roots of the corresponding weights as columns of two matrices with ''N'' columns to obtain the alternative formulation). A compact and elegant derivation can be found in Appel (2015).<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Appel|first=M.|title=Robust Spoofing Detection and Mitigation based on Direction of Arrival Estimation|url=https://elib.dlr.de/99721/1/appel_ion_2015_v05.pdf|journal=Ion GNSS+ 2015|volume=28}}</ref>

== Solution via SVD ==

One solution can be found using a singular value decomposition (SVD).

1. Obtain a matrix <math>\mathbf{B}</math> as follows:

:<math>\mathbf{B} = \sum_{i=1}^{n} a_i \mathbf{w}_i {\mathbf{v}_i}^T</math>

2. Find the [[singular value decomposition]] of <math>\mathbf{B}</math>

:<math>\mathbf{B} = \mathbf{U} \mathbf{S} \mathbf{V}^T</math>

3. The rotation matrix is simply:

:<math>\mathbf{R} = \mathbf{U} \mathbf{M} \mathbf{V}^T</math>

where <math>\mathbf{M} = \operatorname{diag}(\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 & \det(\mathbf{U}) \det(\mathbf{V})\end{bmatrix})</math>
